lxc_7dc8bfa0c3eb94e6.text: First, we look at Japanese greetings and how bowing and greeting words change with time and status.

lxc_1dbbb79df0c7f622.text: Next, we enter a Japanese home and follow the shoes-and-slippers steps.

lxc_8386a02aaadf9c8f.text: Then we sit at the table in Japan and at a restaurant in France.

lxc_83e31ca08f607038.text: Finally, we see why Japan has no tipping custom and how its fast trains stay on time.

lxc_a87fab2966d99250.text: Imagine two people meet at a Japanese office in the morning.

lxc_26cf26d2cb4743aa.text: Later, they meet again in the evening.

lxc_0899e5701c3f4480.text: They do not just say the same "hello" both times.

lxc_94f1e887c430a215.text: A Japanese greeting changes with the time of day and with the people.

lxc_4b63b457b93b9415.text: In Japan, bowing is the common greeting.

lxc_06e4993cc3d900c6.text: But not every bow is the same.

lxc_eb6c4e18054cd686.text: The bow changes with social status, so it depends on who is greeting whom.

lxc_563909d1b8cd7ca8.text: A bow to a senior manager is not the same as a bow to a friend.

lxc_9d9b8b8bfccaaa4a.text: People say "konnichiwa" in the daytime and "konbanwa" in the evening.

lxc_dad03acfb5c1af89.text: They use these words when they meet someone for the first time that day.

lxc_e247ce3cdacce7a2.text: So a Japanese greeting does more than say "I see you."

lxc_f490f6e288ab0ef6.text: It also shows the time of day and how the two people are connected.

lxc_427196c744357c79.text: You can think of it like the address on a letter.

lxc_3051a32aa6f445f9.text: It is short, but it tells you where the letter is going.

lxc_7d268c8d5802c00a.text: In the same way, a short bow tells both people something about their relationship.

lxc_68650307304d5227.text: For a visitor, this has a practical side.

lxc_4646159bbf95674c.text: You do not need a perfect bow.

lxc_73fb0f4888e4ddb9.text: But it helps to notice that greetings in Japan follow the situation.

lxc_6c7cfc6cea474128.text: They are not one fixed action.

lxc_30c96e2e1c165248.text: Now imagine a Japanese colleague invites you to their home.

lxc_9d1f225093bbc865.text: This is a bigger moment than it may seem.

lxc_95aea8f9be482a0e.text: Being invited to a Japanese home is an honour.

lxc_e7f758bbb3feaf82.text: Many Japanese people feel their homes are humble, which means simple or not special enough for guests.

lxc_5944a6ebdf2ff269.text: So when someone opens their home to you, they are giving you something important.

lxc_06ed6f925a72dfbd.text: Inside the home, you will find clear borders, and each border has its own rule.

lxc_9dad665b55746694.text: At the entrance, people take off their shoes.

lxc_6ea73077fd1ec126.text: Then they put on indoor slippers.

lxc_a8bd5ef1f0c16fbc.text: When they step onto tatami, the straw mats on some floors, they take off the slippers too.

lxc_0d74a2bf485ab331.text: People take off their slippers there, and sometimes they put on special bathroom slippers instead.

lxc_8e2a162d1fc80aab.text: So one short walk through a house can mean more than one change of footwear.

lxc_eb3344e2616c7910.text: The rule is not just "no shoes inside."

lxc_45abe226e73ae6cb.text: The rule is that different parts of the home have different steps.

lxc_460b114f514abd52.text: The entrance, the main rooms, the tatami room and the bathroom each have their own.

lxc_fac86064fb71397f.text: Think of it like the doors at an airport.

lxc_2fed8cf1a33714e9.text: You pass one gate and follow one rule.

lxc_9c6bf4991b2d5f41.text: Then you pass the next gate and follow another.

lxc_e89096919c8b9de6.text: A guest who follows these steps shows that they understand the home and respect the invitation.

lxc_0317d0431fa1e4f6.text: At a Japanese meal, the table is a shared space.

lxc_10204542a88016a7.text: Many rules exist to keep that space fair for everyone.

lxc_41d31b72d4e007e6.text: Before eating, people say "itadakimasu," a word of thanks at the start of the meal.

lxc_2544ae795859aac1.text: They also wait until everyone is ready before they start eating.

lxc_583a77bb2eab4f90.text: Nobody runs ahead of the group.

lxc_d8d203d103f07802.text: Everyone takes food from the same plates, so small actions matter.

lxc_c4ed82a2eaa8c7a4.text: If one piece of food is left, it is polite to ask before you take the last bite.

lxc_bee1849ae73a4232.text: Leaving food on your own plate is seen as rude.

lxc_1fdda4787015cbb2.text: Together, these rules work like the rules of a team game.

lxc_5b20c2fbaf9e692e.text: Each person plays their part, so the whole table has a good meal.

lxc_ff3685751a45b934.text: Some rules are more flexible than visitors expect.

lxc_e22bc35e7bb40c89.text: Sushi, for example, can be eaten with chopsticks or with your hands.

lxc_d287d83e29e24ed7.text: So the point is not to make every action strict.

lxc_64b298806dfb5f6d.text: The point is to respect the food and the other people at the table.

lxc_9a76edf023e606ae.text: France shows a different place where manners begin.

lxc_20031f7d7c9f236c.text: In a French restaurant, the rules start at the door, before any food arrives.

lxc_3b717727e0c806f6.text: Staff usually give guests a table.

lxc_dbcb84d4b98be972.text: Customers wait at the entrance until someone takes them to a table.

lxc_658639773dc8981c.text: If you want a different table, you can ask, but you should ask politely.

lxc_bc3a390665b11d52.text: In Japan, the clearest rules are around sharing the food.

lxc_09e077b6b0fc4abc.text: In France, an important rule comes at the start: let the staff guide you.

lxc_acd3e38decd14a73.text: Here is a question many visitors ask: if you do not tip, why would the service be good?

lxc_0a6fb624cd0a7ef4.text: In Japan, tipping is generally not practised.

lxc_2aa5cc46d0319a01.text: Sometimes a service charge is already part of the price.

lxc_25791738eb56c9a8.text: But Japanese service is known for being very polite and careful.

lxc_be6855de4f627894.text: So the missing tip does not mean missing effort.

lxc_326496cf19d19916.text: The reason lies in an idea about customers.

lxc_a66bdccda3dd37f2.text: In Japan, the customer is treated almost like a god.

lxc_242698240be0a0b9.text: Good service is part of the job and part of the price, not an extra that you pay for at the end.

lxc_0866339a1ed90a66.text: If you leave money on the table, it can seem strange, because the work was already expected.

lxc_51b9be35fce49914.text: Paying has its own manners too.

lxc_859de3d7f6373e83.text: It is proper to put your money on a small tray, not to hand it straight to the person.

lxc_d8130d0994a11742.text: Like the slippers at a doorway, the tray is a small step that shows care.

lxc_6b390164c7efaf7a.text: So the link between money and service is different here.

lxc_de592414a61bfc59.text: In some places, a tip is a way to say "thank you for good service."

lxc_c4fd67c8a8783edf.text: In Japan, the thank-you is already part of the system, and the service is the starting point.

lxc_8b532abcd0d183c0.text: All these customs share one habit: careful attention to small steps.

lxc_640d342355aa1c18.text: You can see the same habit in Japan's fast trains.

lxc_e3ac630293928267.text: The Tokaido Shinkansen is a high-speed line in Japan.

lxc_01aee76fd5c9460d.text: In 2024, it ran 383 trains a day and carried about 460,000 passengers.

lxc_c4f028a4bb77e3f2.text: Those trains had an average delay of just 1.4 minutes per train.

lxc_e5470d350d2ee316.text: Now think about the size of the job.

lxc_9e597be0293318a3.text: If 460,000 people share 383 trains, that is about 1,200 people per train on average.

lxc_ecddfa68bf8fa6ab.text: Each person must get on and off quickly, every train must leave on time, and this happens all day.

lxc_2932d082f6e697dc.text: This is where the small habits matter.

lxc_95290b015c972250.text: A delay on one train can spread to the next one, like a line of people at a shop.

lxc_3a1847ccc94ec4b0.text: When one person stops, everyone behind them waits too.

lxc_16ed76bdcd4cf386.text: So a short average delay is not only about fast machines.

lxc_50ffd6148ac59993.text: It also depends on many small, careful actions, repeated hundreds of times a day.

lxc_53b2483b41c3295a.text: Bowing to the right person, changing slippers at the right door and leaving a train exactly on time may seem very different.

lxc_649758b1a9f2bb77.text: But they all show the same thing: people paying close attention to the small step in front of them.
